summary: Describes the algorithms that implement Boneh-Franklin and Boneh-Boyen identity-based encryption, in which a person's identity, such as an email address, serves as their public key. It is based partly on Voltage Security's IBCS documents. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Normally you need a special key to send someone a secret. Here, their email address can act as the key, which is easier to arrange.

questions: what is a private key generator
subtitle: The algorithms for encrypting to someone using only their identity, such as an email address, as the public key.

tldr.problem: In ordinary public-key systems the sender must first obtain the recipient's randomly generated key, which requires some prior interaction or a directory lookup.
tldr.mechanism: In identity-based encryption (IBE) a public key is calculated from an identity string and public parameters. The recipient later gets the matching private key from a Private-key Generator, and RFC 5091 specifies the Boneh-Franklin (BF) and Boneh-Boyen (BB1) algorithms on type-1 supersingular curves.
tldr.outcome: A sender needs only the recipient's identity and the public parameters. The IESG note warns that the document had limited IETF review and that readers should evaluate it carefully.

sections.title: Identity-Based Encryption
sections.content:
This document says it specifies two mathematical algorithms for identity-based encryption (IBE), the systems of Boneh and Franklin (BF) and Boneh and Boyen (BB1). It is partly based on Voltage Security's IBCS #1 v2 document. An IESG note says that because of its specialized nature the document received limited review within the IETF, and readers should carefully evaluate its value for implementation and deployment.

IBE is public-key technology, but keys are calculated instead of generated randomly. A public key is calculated from an identity, and the private key from the public key, both as needed. That removes the need for sender and receiver to interact, directly or through a directory server, before sending a secure message. Examples of identities are an individual, group or role identifier.

IBE is used only for encryption. If digital signatures are needed, they must come from an additional mechanism.
sections.eli5: Your email address is already known to everyone, so it can be the lock. Nobody has to ask you for a lock first.

sections.title: The Two Servers: PKG and PPS
sections.content:
A complete IBE messaging system needs two components. The Private-key Generator (PKG) holds a master secret used to generate individual private keys. It authenticates a user who requests a key and then returns it. The Public Parameter Server (PPS) is a well-known location that distributes the public parameters and the PKG's policy information.

The RFC suggests one PKG/PPS per name space, such as a DNS zone, so it is clear which public parameters to use for a given identity. PPS servers and PKG servers MUST support TLS 1.1, and the URI used to obtain public parameters MUST be authenticated. Private keys MUST travel over a secure protocol.

The PKG may let someone other than the recipient obtain some private keys. The RFC gives the example of a mail filtering appliance that scans encrypted messages for viruses.
sections.eli5: One office hands out the rule book that anyone can read, and another office hands out your personal key after checking your ID.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving a Message
sections.content:
To send, the user first obtains the recipient's public parameters from a PPS. The sender then chooses a content encryption key (CEK), encrypts the message with it, and encrypts the CEK with the recipient's IBE public key. IBE-encrypted messages can use standard formats such as the Cryptographic Message Syntax (RFC 3852).

To read, the recipient parses the message to find the URI of the public parameters and the identity used. The recipient fetches the parameters from the PPS, then authenticates to the PKG and receives the private key over HTTPS. The private key decrypts the CEK, which decrypts the content.

The PKG's authentication matters most. The security of the whole system depends on how strongly users are authenticated before receiving private keys, much as with certificates.
sections.eli5: Put the message in a box with a lock made from the recipient's address. They show their ID to the key office, get the key, and open the box.

sections.title: Curves and Pairings
sections.content:
Both systems rely on a bilinear pairing: the Tate pairing (or a modified version) is an efficiently computable map that is linear in both arguments and believed hard to invert. The document restricts itself to type-1 curves, which are curves y^2 = x^3 + 1 over a prime field for primes p congruent to 11 modulo 12. They are supersingular and always have embedding degree 2.

Type-1 curves are freshly generated at random for each application rather than standardized. Sections 3 and 4 give the supporting algorithms: point multiplication, the Miller algorithm for the pairing, hashing to an integer range, hashing a string onto a curve subgroup, and canonical encodings of field elements. Curves of other classes are unsupported.
sections.eli5: It uses a special kind of math puzzle on curves that can mix two secrets into a third one in a way that is easy to do forward but very hard to undo.

sections.title: The BF and BB1 Cryptosystems
sections.content:
Each system has the same stages: setup, public key derivation, private key extraction, encryption and decryption. Setup randomly picks a master secret and public parameters. The security parameter n MUST be one of 1024, 2048, 3072, 7680 or 15360.

In BF, the public key Q_id comes from hashing the identity onto the curve. To encrypt, the plaintext MUST be a random symmetric session key. The result is a triple (U, V, W) built from a random value, a hash of the plaintext, a pairing of the public parameters with Q_id, and XOR masking. BB1 follows the practical implementation in the Boneh-Boyen paper and uses its own setup, extraction and encryption algorithms.

Section 8 gives an ASN.1 module for the encodings, and Section 7 gives test data for the main algorithms.
sections.eli5: Both recipes mix the address, a random number and the key office's secret into a scrambled box. Only the matching key can unscramble it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC assumes five strength levels: 80, 112, 128, 192 and 256 bits. The 80-bit level SHOULD NOT be used to protect information whose useful life extends past the year 2010. If an IBE key carries a symmetric key stronger than itself, the weaker IBE key limits the security.

Identities are hashed with NIST algorithms. Collisions in SHA-1 could in theory give two identities the same private key, but any protocol using IBE MUST define identities so that collisions are useless to an attacker. Random values MUST come from a source of adequate security.

The PKG and its administrators can create any private key, so controls and logging SHOULD exist. Alternatively, a master secret can be destroyed after keys are made, which rules out key recovery. If recovery is not wanted, the identity format SHOULD include a short-lived component, such as a validity period, to allow rekeying.
sections.eli5: The key office could in theory make a key for anyone, so it must be watched closely. Using addresses that expire lets you swap keys if one gets stolen.
